    Slide 3

    Asymptotes of Functions (Recap)

    An asymptote is a line that a graph approaches but never actually reaches. As \(x\) or \(y\) grows large (positively or negatively), the function’s graph gets arbitrarily close to the asymptote.

    Types of Asymptotes 1. Vertical Asymptotes 2. Horizontal Asymptotes 3. Slant/Oblique Asymptotes

    Footer: Ikechi Ndukwe | MA I | Lab 13 (December 3, 2025) | 3 / 14

    Slide 4

    Vertical Asymptote (VA) (Recap)

    Definition: A vertical asymptote occurs at \(x = a\) if the function values grow without bound as \(x\) approaches \(a\).

    \[ \lim_{x \to a^-} f(x) = \pm\infty \quad \text{or} \quad \lim_{x \to a^+} f(x) = \pm\infty \]

    • For rational functions, vertical asymptotes occur at values of \(x\) where the denominator is zero and the numerator is nonzero.
    • Solve \(d(x) = 0\) for the denominator \(d(x)\).

    Example: \[ f(x) = \frac{3x}{x - 2} \implies \text{Vertical asymptote at } x = 2. \]

    Footer: Ikechi Ndukwe | MA I | Lab 13 (December 3, 2025) | 4 / 14

    Slide 5

    Horizontal Asymptote (HA) (Recap)

    Definition: A horizontal asymptote describes the end behavior of a function as \(x \to \pm\infty\).

    \[ \lim_{x \to \infty} f(x) = L \quad \text{or} \quad \lim_{x \to -\infty} f(x) = L \implies \text{Horizontal asymptote: } y = L. \]

    For Rational Functions: * If \(\deg(n) < \deg(d)\): \(y = 0\). * If \(\deg(n) = \deg(d)\): \[ y = \frac{\text{leading coefficient of numerator (n)}}{\text{leading coefficient of denominator (d)}} \] * If \(\deg(n) > \deg(d)\): no horizontal asymptote.

    Example: \[ f(x) = \frac{4x^2 - 1}{2x^2 + 5} \implies y = \frac{4}{2} = 2. \]

    Footer: Ikechi Ndukwe | MA I | Lab 13 (December 3, 2025) | 5 / 14

    Slide 6

    Slant/Oblique Asymptote (SA) (Recap)

    Definition: A slant or oblique asymptote occurs when the graph approaches a non-horizontal line \(y = mx + b\) as \(x \to \pm\infty\).

    \[ \lim_{x \to \infty} [f(x) - (mx + b)] = 0 \]

    When Do They Occur? * For rational functions, if \[ \deg(n) = \deg(d) + 1, \] then dividing \(n(x)\) by \(d(x)\) yields \[ f(x) = mx + b + \frac{r(x)}{d(x)}. \] * The line \(y = mx + b\) is the slant asymptote.

    Footer: Ikechi Ndukwe | MA I | Lab 13 (December 3, 2025) | 6 / 14

    Slide 7

    Limit for Indeterminate Form \(1^{\infty}\)

    Corollary Suppose \(\lim_{x \to c} g(x) = 1\), and \(\lim_{x \to c} h(x) = \infty\). Then

    \[ \begin{aligned} \lim_{x \to c} [g(x)]^{h(x)} &= \lim_{x \to c} [1 + (g(x) - 1)]^{h(x)} \\ &= \lim_{x \to c} e^{h(x)(g(x)-1)} \\ &= e^{\lim_{x \to c} [h(x)(g(x) - 1)]} \end{aligned} \]

    Footer: Ikechi Ndukwe | MA I | Lab 13 (December 3, 2025) | 7 / 14

    Slide 9

    Continuity

    A function \(f(x)\) is said to be continuous at an interior point \(x = c\) of its domain if and only if it meets the following three conditions:

    1. \(f(c)\) exists (\(c\) lies in the domain of \(f\))
    2. \(\lim_{x \to c} f(x)\) exists (\(f\) has a limit as \(x\) tends to \(c\))
    3. \(\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)\) (the limit equals the function value)

    Footer: Ikechi Ndukwe | MA I | Lab 13 (December 3, 2025) | 9 / 14

    Slide 10

    Properties of Continuous Functions

    If the functions \(f\) and \(g\) are continuous at \(x = c\), then the following combinations are continuous at \(x = c\).

    1. \(f + g\)
    2. \(f - g\)
    3. \(k \cdot f\), for any number \(k\)
    4. \(f \cdot g\)
    5. \(f / g\), provided \(g(c) \neq 0\)
    6. \(f^n\), \(n\) a positive integer
    7. \(\sqrt[n]{f}\), provided it is defined on an open interval containing \(c\), where \(n\) is a positive integer

    Footer: Ikechi Ndukwe | MA I | Lab 13 (December 3, 2025) | 10 / 14

    Slide 11

    Types of Discontinuity

    [Image Description]: The slide contains a composite figure labeled “Figure: Types of Discontinuity” displaying four different graphs plotted on Cartesian coordinate systems (\(x\) vs \(y\)), illustrating different ways a function can be discontinuous.

    • (a) Jump Discontinuity: The graph consists of two linear segments. As \(x\) approaches \(0\) from the left, the line approaches a positive value (approx \(y=1\)). As \(x\) leaves \(0\) to the right, a new line starts from a higher positive value (approx \(y=2\)) and continues upwards. There is a visible gap or “jump” between the two segments at \(x=0\).
    • (b) Removable Discontinuity: The graph shows a single straight line passing through the origin. However, at a specific point on the line (appearing to be in the positive quadrant), there is a hollow circle (an open dot), indicating the function is undefined or has a hole at that specific \(x\) value, despite the limit existing.
    • (c) Infinite Discontinuity: The graph shows a curve (similar to \(y=1/x^2\) or similar rational function). As \(x\) approaches \(0\) from either the left or the right, the curve shoots vertically upwards towards positive infinity. It never touches the y-axis, indicating a vertical asymptote at \(x=0\).
    • (f) Oscillating / Wild Discontinuity: The graph (labeled with a lower letter, likely ‘f’ or ‘d’) displays a function that oscillates rapidly. As \(x\) approaches \(0\) from the right, the frequency of the oscillations increases infinitely (similar to \(y = \sin(1/x)\)), creating a solid block of waves near the y-axis, making it impossible to define a single limit.

    Text Content: 1. Jump Discontinuity 2. Removable Discontinuity 3. Infinite Discontinuity 4. Oscillating / Wild Discontinuity
